hero.caption: The wave goes. The rope stays.

intro: Flick one end of a rope. A bump runs down to the far end, but the rope itself doesn't go anywhere. That's a **wave**: an oscillation that **spreads through space**. This chapter teaches waves step by step: what they are, how to describe them (**A**, **λ**, **T**, **f**), the speed formula **v = f·λ**, and the two flavours, transverse and longitudinal.

goals.title: In this chapter you'll learn to
items: explain a **wave** as an oscillation that spreads through space, passing energy along **without moving matter**;

describe a wave with **amplitude A**, **wavelength λ**, **period T** and **frequency f = 1/T**, and measure them in the wave lab and from pictures of a wave (the graphs of y against x and y against t come in *A wave in space and time*);
use the wave speed formula **v = f·λ** (and rearrange it for f or λ);
tell **transverse** from **longitudinal** waves, with examples: rope, sound, earthquake P and S waves.

warmup.say: You shake a rope's end. Then shake twice as often!
warmup.question:
You shake one end of a long rope up and down. Now you shake it **twice as often** (double the frequency).

The wave travels along the rope...
verdicts: Yes! The rope decides, not your hand.
warmup.explain: **The medium sets the speed.** How fast a bump runs along a rope depends on the rope (how tight it is, how heavy), not on how you shake it. So when the frequency doubles but v stays put, the **wavelength must halve**: λ = v/f. With v = {labV} m/s, going from {labF} Hz to {f2} Hz shrinks λ from {labLam} m to {lam2} m. You'll see it in the lab.

lab.scene: A rope of beads carrying a wave, with a ruler showing one wavelength
lab.ruler_long: one wavelength = {n} m (longer than the rope)
lab.status_t: Transverse: the beads move sideways, across the direction the wave travels.
lab.status_l: Longitudinal: the beads shuffle back and forth along the direction of travel. Look for squeezed (compressions) and stretched (rarefactions) regions.
lab.status_track_t: The yellow bead only moves up and down. The wave runs past it. Nothing travels along the rope.
lab.status_track_l: The yellow bead only shuffles back and forth around the same spot. The wave runs past it.

learn1.title: What is a wave?
learn1.body:
Think of the rope as a row of little **oscillators**, like the masses on springs from *Push back* and *The shape of a wobble*. Each piece is tied to its neighbours. Shake the first piece and it pulls the second, which starts moving a moment later, and pulls the third, and so on. The oscillation is **passed down the line**. That is a **wave**: the spreading of an oscillation in space. The material the wave runs through (the rope, the air, the rock) is called the **medium**.

The lab below is a rope of 41 beads, each tugging on its neighbours. Press **Shake from rest** and watch the disturbance run to the right.
learn1.tasks:
**Try this:** press **Track one bead**. A yellow bead is picked out. Watch it, then compare it with the readout **wave pattern has travelled**. The bead only goes up and down in place, while the pattern races along the rope.

The oscillation travels. The matter doesn't.

check.q: A wave runs along a rope from left to right. A bit of red paint marks one piece of the rope. What does the red mark do?
choices: It moves up and down around its own spot
It travels to the right with the wave
check.why: Each piece of rope just **oscillates around its own position**. The wave pattern travels along the rope, the paint mark doesn't.
whyNot: The wave travels, the rope doesn't. If the mark went along, the rope would pile up at the far end.
Nothing in the rope travels left either. Think about what each piece of rope actually does.
It isn't still: the wave is pieces of rope moving. What does one piece do while the pattern passes?

learn2.title: Describing a wave
learn2.body:
Five quantities describe a wave.
- **Displacement y**: how far a piece of the medium is from its rest position, in metres (m).
- **Amplitude A**: the **largest** displacement, in m. Measure from the middle line up to a crest (not from trough to crest).
- **Wavelength λ**: the distance along the wave between two neighbouring crests (or any two neighbouring points that are doing exactly the same thing), in m. You read it from a **snapshot** (y against position x).
- **Period T**: the time for **one full oscillation**, in seconds (s). You read it from a **time graph** (y against t) of one piece of the medium.

**Frequency f** is the number of oscillations per second. Its unit is the hertz, 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹.
learn2.after:
**Phase:** two points are **in phase** if they are at the same stage of their oscillation (e.g. both at a crest, or both moving up through the middle). Points exactly one wavelength apart are in phase. Points half a wavelength apart do the opposite of each other.

The **frequency is set by the source** (your hand). The wave speed does **not** depend on the amplitude: a bigger shake makes taller crests, not faster ones. The lab shows the same ideas live.
learn2.tasks: **Try this in the lab:** the ruler at the bottom shows one wavelength. Hit **Freeze** and slide **A**: only the height of the crests changes. Slide **f** up: T gets shorter and the crests bunch together, so λ gets shorter (keep v fixed). Assumptions: the rope is {rope} m long, no damping.

check.q: In a snapshot of a wave, a crest is at x = {x1} m and the next crest is at x = {x2} m. The crests reach +{sA} m and the troughs −{sA} m (measured from the middle line). What are λ and A?
check.why: λ is the **distance between neighbouring crests**: {x2} − {x1} = **{sLam} m**. A is measured from the middle line to a crest: **{sA} m** (the trough-to-crest height {sAbad} m is 2A).
whyNot: {sAbad} m is measured from trough to crest. A is measured from a different starting line.
{x2} m is where the second crest sits, not the gap to it. λ is a distance between two crests.
That is half the crest-to-crest gap: the way from a crest to a trough. Check what λ counts.

check2.q: A piece of rope goes through {oN} full oscillations in {oT} s. What are its period T and the frequency f?
check2.why: T = {oT} s ÷ {oN} = **{oPer} s**, and f = 1/T = 1/{oPer} = **{oF} Hz**. (Check: {oN} oscillations in {oT} s is {oF} per second.)
whyNot: You swapped T and f. T is the time for ONE oscillation; f is how many fit in one second.
You multiplied {oN} by {oT}. To get the time for one oscillation, divide the total time by the count.
T looks fine, but f is not equal to T. Use f = 1/T instead of copying the number.

examples.title: Watch it done, step by step

items.title: Example 1: find the wave speed
items.problem: A wave on a long spring has frequency **{we1f} Hz** and wavelength **{we1lam} m**. Find its speed and its period.
steps: Write the formula from the booklet: **v = f·λ**.
Substitute (both already in SI units): v = {we1f} × {we1lam}.
The period is the inverse of the frequency: T = 1/f = 1/{we1f}.

items.title: Example 2: wavelength of a sound
items.problem: A loudspeaker plays the note A at **{soundF} Hz**. Sound travels in air at 20 °C at **{soundV} m/s**. Find the wavelength.
steps: Rearrange v = f·λ for the unknown: **λ = v/f**.
Units: (m/s) ÷ (1/s) = m, so the answer is a length, as it should be.

items.title: Example 3: from the period to the speed
items.problem: Ripples pass a floating cork, which bobs up and down once every **{we3T} s**. Neighbouring crests are **{we3lam} m** apart. Find the speed of the ripples.
steps: The time for one bob is the period: T = {we3T} s. Convert to a frequency: **f = 1/T** = 1/{we3T} = {we3f} Hz.
Check with the other recipe: in one period the crest moves one wavelength, so v = λ/T = {we3lam}/{we3T}. Same answer.

learn3.title: The wave speed v = f·λ
learn3.lead: How fast does the wave pattern travel? Tap the right move at each step to get the formula yourself.
learn3.rule:
$ v = f·λ

Rearranged: **λ = v/f** and **f = v/λ**. In SI units, v is in m/s, f in Hz and λ in m.

**Who decides what?** The **source** sets the frequency (your hand shakes f times a second). The **medium** sets the speed (the rope's tension and mass, the air's temperature). The wavelength then has no choice: λ = v/f. Shake faster and the wave is just as fast but its wavelength is shorter. (The full wave equation y(x, t) comes in the chapter *A wave in space and time*.)

check.q: A wave on a rope travels at {c4v} m/s and the source shakes at {c4f} Hz. What is the wavelength?
check.why: λ = v/f = {c4v} / {c4f} = **{c4lam} m**. The others come from multiplying, flipping or adding the numbers.
whyNot: That is v × f = {c4w1}. Multiplying gives the wrong unit: (m/s) × Hz is not a length.
That is f/v, the formula upside down. Check the unit: Hz ÷ (m/s) is not metres.
You added {c4v} and {c4f}. m/s and Hz have different units, so you can't add them.

game.title: Time the crest: measure a speed yourself
game.lead: The source on the left shakes at **f = {gF} Hz**, and the rope's speed is a secret. The yellow dot rides the **first crest**. Markers **A** and **B** are **{gD} m** apart. Press **Shake!**, then tap **Start clock** as the crest passes A and **Stop clock** as it passes B. Your taps will be a little late, but both are late by about the same amount, so the difference is still good. Measure v = d/Δt to within **{gTol}%** of the true speed. A new rope has a new secret speed.
game.scene: A rope with markers A and B and a yellow dot riding the first crest
game.ok: Within the tolerance. You measured a wave's speed!
game.too_fast: Your speed came out too high: the clock was too short. Stop it later, or start it earlier.
game.too_slow: Your speed came out too low: the clock was too long. Stop it sooner, or start it later.
game.truth: The rope's true speed is {v} m/s. Check with the other recipe: the wavelength was λ = {lam} m, so f·λ = {f} Hz × {lam} m = {prod} m/s.
game.win: You found the speed from **distance ÷ time**, the way you'd time any moving thing. The same speed also comes out of **v = f·λ**: the source shakes at f = {gF} Hz, and the wavelength is however far the crest gets in one period. Two recipes, one speed. (Reduced motion: use the freeze buttons, which show the moment the crest reaches A and B.)

steps.prompt: The source shakes with period T. In exactly **one period** T, how far does a crest travel along the rope?
steps.then: **One wavelength λ.** After one full shake the source makes the next crest, so the first crest has moved ahead by exactly the gap between crests.

steps.prompt: Speed is distance divided by time. With distance λ and time T, the wave speed is...
steps.then: **v = λ/T.** Check the units: metres per second.

steps.prompt: Frequency is f = 1/T. So λ/T can also be written as...
steps.then:
**v = f·λ.** That's the booklet's formula.

With it you can find any one of the three: **λ = v/f** or **f = v/λ**. And since the medium fixes v, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.

learn4.title: Transverse and longitudinal waves
learn4.lead:
The lab can shake the beads in two ways. Press **Longitudinal**, then press it back to **Transverse** and compare.

- **Transverse wave:** the pieces oscillate **at right angles** to the direction the wave travels (a rope; a stadium wave looks the same).
- **Longitudinal wave:** the pieces oscillate **along** the direction the wave travels. You get squeezed regions (**compressions**) and stretched regions (**rarefactions**). Sound in air and a pushed long spring are longitudinal. The **wavelength** of a longitudinal wave is the distance from one compression to the next compression.

**Earthquakes** send out both kinds through the rock: **P waves** are longitudinal (and faster), **S waves** are transverse (and slower).
learn4.tasks: In the longitudinal view, find where the beads bunch up (a compression). *(For the picture the shuffle is drawn smaller than the real amplitude when the wavelength is short, so beads never pass through each other.)* Then do the sort cards below.

check0.q: In a longitudinal wave on a long spring, which distance is one wavelength?
choices: From one compression to the next compression
From a compression to the next rarefaction
The distance one coil moves back and forth
The whole length of the spring
check0.why: The pattern repeats from one **compression to the next compression** (or one rarefaction to the next). That distance is λ. Half of it separates a compression from a rarefaction.
whyNot: That is only half the repeat distance. The pattern has to look exactly the same again.
How far one coil shuffles is the size of the oscillation, not the length of the wave.
The wave pattern repeats many times along the spring, so the spring's length isn't λ.

check.q: Which statement about earthquake waves is correct?
choices: P waves are longitudinal and S waves are transverse
P waves are transverse and S waves are longitudinal
check.why: **P** waves (primary, faster) are **longitudinal**, like sound. **S** waves (secondary, slower) are **transverse**: the rock shakes sideways.
whyNot: Then P and S would be the same kind of wave, yet they arrive at different speeds. Look back at what the chapter said about each of them.
Check the order. Which of P and S is the fast one, and which kind of wave does sound make? Match them up.
Then P and S would be the same kind of wave, yet one is faster than the other. Look back at what the chapter said about each of them.

bigidea.title: Energy moves, matter doesn't
bigidea.lead: A wave carries **energy** from A to B. Does it also carry **matter** from A to B? Tap each card to find out.

cards.label: Stadium wave
cards.why: Each person stands up and sits down in their own seat. The wave runs round the stadium, the people don't.

cards.label: Flick along a rope
cards.why: The bump runs from one end to the other, but each piece of rope only moves up and down. Track a bead in the lab to see it.

cards.label: Sound from a speaker
cards.why: Air molecules shuffle back and forth a tiny distance. The compression travels at about {soundV} m/s in air at 20 °C, but no air travels from the speaker to your ear.

cards.label: Water in a hose
cards.why: This is a flow, not a wave: the water itself moves from the tap to the end of the hose.

cards.label: Cork on a pond
cards.why: A ripple passes and the cork bobs, staying roughly where it is. The ripple spreads, the cork doesn't follow it.

cards.label: A thrown ball
cards.why: Matter and energy both go from A to B. A ball is not a wave.

bigidea.after: A wave moves **energy and a pattern**, not material. Why? Each bead pulls on its neighbour, which starts to move a moment later. That's a system of **coupled oscillators**: bead 1 passes the shake to bead 2, bead 2 to bead 3, and so on, while every bead stays near its own home. Energy is handed down the line like a baton.

labels.score: You got {right} of {n}. Check the solutions for any you missed.
labels.perfect: All {n} right! You are ready for this in a test.

items.q: A point on a rope oscillates with period T = {p1T} s. What is the frequency?
items.solution: Formula (booklet): f = 1/T. Substitute: f = 1/{p1T} s = **{p1f} Hz**. Sense check: a short period means many oscillations per second, so a big f is right.
whyNot: {p1w1} Hz is the period T = {p1T} s read as a frequency. f = 1/T = {p1f} Hz.
{p1w2} would be {p1f} Hz converted to kHz but still labelled Hz. Keep Hz: f = {p1f} Hz.
{p1w3} Hz is ten times too big: check the decimal places in T. 1/{p1T} = {p1f} Hz.

items.q: A wave on a string has frequency {p2f} Hz and wavelength {p2lam} m. What is its speed?
items.solution: Formula (booklet): v = f·λ. Substitute: v = {p2f} Hz × {p2lam} m = **{p2v} m/s**. Units: Hz × m = (1/s) × m = m/s. Sense check: a few metres per second is typical for a wave on a rope or spring.
whyNot: That is f ÷ λ. The formula multiplies: v = f·λ = {p2v} m/s.
That is λ ÷ f, upside down. v = f·λ = {p2v} m/s.
That adds f and λ, but Hz and m can't be added. v = f·λ = {p2v} m/s.

items.q: The time graph of one piece of a medium repeats every {p3T} s. The wave speed is {p3v} m/s. What is the wavelength?
items.hint: The repeat time is the period T. Then f = 1/T and λ = v/f.
items.solution: The repeat time is the period, T = {p3T} s, so f = 1/T = 1/{p3T} = {p3f} Hz. Then v = f·λ gives λ = v/f = {p3v} m/s ÷ {p3f} Hz = **{p3lam} m**. Shortcut: λ = v·T gives the same, because in one period the wave moves one wavelength.
whyNot: {p3w1} is v ÷ T, which is v·f and not a length. λ = v/f = v·T = {p3lam} m.
{p3w2} is T ÷ v, upside down. λ = v/f = v·T = {p3lam} m.
That adds v and T, but m/s and s can't be added. λ = v·T = {p3lam} m.

items.q: Which of these is a transverse wave?
choices: A P wave in an earthquake
Compressions running along a pushed spring
items.hint: Transverse: the pieces oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel.
items.solution: In a transverse wave the pieces oscillate at right angles to the direction of travel: that is the **rope wave**. Sound, P waves and compressions on a spring all have the pieces shuffling along the direction of travel, so they are **longitudinal**.
whyNot: Sound is longitudinal: the air molecules shuffle along the direction it travels.
P waves are longitudinal (compressions, like sound). The transverse earthquake waves are the S waves.
Compressions on a spring are longitudinal: the coils move back and forth along the spring.

items.q: A wave passes a cork floating on a pond. What does the wave transfer from one place to another?
choices: Energy, with essentially no net movement of water
items.hint: Think about what the cork does.
items.solution: A wave passes energy along through coupled oscillators: each piece is pulled by its neighbour and pulls the next. The water and cork only move in small circles around their positions. So the wave transfers **energy, with essentially no net movement of water**.
whyNot: It's the other way round: the wave carries energy, and the water stays near its place (it moves in small circles, with almost no drift).
Energy yes, but the water doesn't travel with the wave: the cork bobs around the same spot instead of drifting along.
A wave does transfer energy: that is how it can lift the cork, shake a boat or move your eardrum.

story.title: Waves that look inside the Earth

frames.text: A huge earthquake shakes Assam, in north-east India. Instruments around the world, **seismographs**, record wiggly lines of the ground shaking.

Richard Dixon Oldham, a geologist who studied the Indian earthquake, sorts the wiggles. In the records from far away he sees **three kinds of arrival**: a first small shudder, a second one later, and a big slow rolling one last (the **surface wave**, which runs along the ground instead of deep inside).

The first two are **body waves**, which travel through the inside of the Earth: **P** (primary, first, longitudinal) and **S** (secondary, second, transverse). The delay between them tells you the distance (see the bonus at the end of the chapter if you want to do the sums).

In 1906 Oldham saw that waves crossing deep through the Earth arrived late, and he argued the planet has a distinct **core**. Later work found that S waves **never get through the outer core**: it must be liquid.

story.question: S waves are transverse: the rock must spring back when pushed **sideways**, and a liquid can't do that. Seismometers on the far side of the Earth never record S waves that went through the core. What does that tell us?
choices: Part of the Earth's interior is liquid
The core is made of something that absorbs sound
S waves are too slow to cross the planet
story.explain: Liquids don't resist being sheared, so a **transverse** wave can't be passed along. P waves, which are compressions, do get through a liquid (slowed down). Together, the missing S waves and the bent, delayed P waves are how we know about the Earth's core without ever going there. (Details: Oldham's 1900 and 1906 papers; the liquid outer core was firmly established over the following decades.)

sim.title: Wave on a String
sim.body:
Shake the end of a string by hand or with an oscillator. Change the frequency, amplitude, damping and tension, and use the ruler and timer to measure λ, T and the speed. Does v = f·λ hold? Predict first, then check. Try changing only the tension: what does it do to the speed?

*Tip: on a phone, turn it sideways.*
sim.attribution: Simulation by PhET Interactive Simulations, University of Colorado Boulder (phet.colorado.edu). Opens on the PhET website.

manga.title: The wave that left everyone behind
manga.body: Draw a 4-panel strip about a stadium wave. **Panel 1:** one hero stands up in the crowd, a ripple starting. **Panel 2:** the ripple passes along the rows, each person standing and sitting in their own seat. **Panel 3:** an aerial view where the wave has gone a quarter of the way round but nobody has left their seat. **Panel 4:** the hero looks at a tiny label: wave speed = f × λ. Add speed lines for the wave, and none for the people.

summary.title: Summary card
items: A **wave** is an oscillation that spreads through space. It carries **energy**, not matter: the pieces of the medium (**coupled oscillators**) only oscillate around their place.

**Amplitude A** (m): largest displacement. **Wavelength λ** (m): distance between neighbouring crests, read from a snapshot. **Period T** (s): time for one oscillation, read from a time graph. **Phase:** points at the same stage of their oscillation are in phase (one wavelength apart); half a wavelength apart they do the opposite.
**Frequency:** f = 1/T, in Hz (= s⁻¹). The **source** sets f.
**Wave speed:** v = f·λ, so λ = v/f and f = v/λ. The **medium** sets v, not the amplitude.
**Transverse:** oscillation at right angles to the travel direction (rope). **Longitudinal:** along it (sound). Earthquake **P** waves are longitudinal and faster, **S** waves transverse and slower.

items.q: A wave has frequency 5 Hz and wavelength 0.4 m. Its speed is...
whyNot: That is f ÷ λ. The formula multiplies: v = f·λ.
That is λ ÷ f, upside down. v = f·λ.
That adds f and λ, but Hz and m can't be added. Multiply: v = f·λ.

items.q: Sound in air at 20 °C (take v = {soundV} m/s) of frequency {q2f} Hz has a wavelength of about...
items.why: λ = v/f = {soundV} / {q2f} = **{q2lam} m**. The others come from flipping or mis-scaling the formula.
whyNot: {q2w1} is f ÷ v, the formula flipped. λ = v/f = {q2lam} m.
{q2w2} m is v + f: you added the speed and the frequency, but m/s and Hz cannot be added. λ = v/f = {q2lam} m.
{q2w3} is the frequency, in Hz, not a length. λ = v/f = {q2lam} m.

items.q: When a sound wave passes, the air molecules move...
choices: back and forth along the direction the wave travels
up and down across the direction the wave travels
steadily from the source to your ear
items.why: Sound is **longitudinal**: the molecules shuffle along the line of travel, making compressions and rarefactions. They don't travel to your ear, only the wave does.
whyNot: Up and down is a transverse wave, like a rope. Sound is longitudinal: the shuffle is along the travel direction.
That would be wind. In a sound wave only the pattern travels; each molecule just shuffles around its place.
No circles: the molecules shuffle back and forth along a line, in the direction the wave travels.

labels.done: Done. Go again for a perfect run?

bonus.title: BONUS
bonus.note: Beyond the syllabus: calculations and puzzles for when you want a challenge. Not needed for your tests.

quake.title: The earthquake clock
quake.say: A seismometer feels the S wave {qDt} s after the P wave!
quake.lead: An earthquake sends out two kinds of wave through the rock. **P waves** (primary) are longitudinal: the rock is squeezed and stretched along the direction of travel, like sound. They're faster. **S waves** (secondary) are transverse: the rock shakes sideways. They're slower. Assumptions (typical crust values): **v_{P} ≈ {vP} km/s, v_{S} ≈ {vS} km/s**, straight-line paths, both waves leave at the same instant. One station records the S wave **{qDt} s** after the P wave.
quake.question: How far away is the earthquake?
verdicts: Too close. That would be the distance S travels in {qDt} s alone:
steps: **Travel times:** the quake is a distance d away. P arrives after t_{P} = d/v_{P}, S after t_{S} = d/v_{S}.
**The gap:** Δt = t_{S} − t_{P} = d·(1/v_{S} − 1/v_{P}). The delay grows in proportion to the distance: each extra km adds 1/{vS} − 1/{vP} ≈ {gapS} s.
**Check:** t_{P} = {qDist}/{vP} = {tP} s and t_{S} = {qDist}/{vS} = {tS} s, and {tS} − {tP} = {qDt} s. ✓ With these speeds, every second of delay means about **{rule} km** of distance.
quake.after: So yes, a delay of {qDt} s puts the quake about {qDist} km away. Real speeds vary with depth and rock type, so seismologists use several stations, each giving a distance circle; where the circles meet is the epicentre.

challenge.title: Thick rope, thin rope
challenge.lead: A thick rope is tied to a thin one, and your hand shakes the thick end at a steady f = {cF} Hz. Waves run along the thick rope at **{thickV} m/s**, then cross the knot onto the thin rope, where they run at **{thinV} m/s** (a lighter rope at the same tension is faster).
challenge.question: As the wave crosses the knot, which one stays **the same**?
choices: None of them stay the same
verdicts: Yes! And that settles the other two.
One of them survives the knot:
challenge.explain: The knot is shaken by the thick rope, and it shakes the thin rope, so both ropes wiggle at the **same frequency**: f = {cF} Hz. If the knot gained or lost cycles, a piece of rope would have to appear or vanish. The speed is set by each rope, and then λ = v/f has no choice: thick rope λ = {thickV}/{cF} = **{thickLam} m**, thin rope λ = {thinV}/{cF} = **{thinLam} m**. Same f, faster v, so a longer wavelength.

snapshot.aria: Snapshot graph of a transverse wave: displacement y against position x. The wave is a smooth up-and-down curve around a dashed middle line. The amplitude A is marked from the middle line up to a crest. The wavelength is marked between two neighbouring crests.
snapshot.caption: **A snapshot of a transverse wave** (y against x): the wave frozen at one moment. **A** is measured from the middle line up to a crest (not trough to crest). **λ** is the distance between two neighbouring crests, or any two neighbouring points doing the same thing. The period **T** is not in this picture: it comes from a time graph of one piece of the medium (y against t).

long.aria: Two rows of dots. The top row shows spring coils at rest, evenly spaced. The bottom row shows the same coils with a longitudinal wave: the coils are bunched close together at the compressions and spread out at the rarefactions. The wavelength is marked from one compression to the next compression.
long.caption: **A longitudinal wave on a spring.** Each coil shuffles back and forth along the spring, so the coils bunch up in **compressions** and spread out in **rarefactions**. One wavelength **λ** is the distance from one compression to the **next compression**. Sound in air looks the same, with air molecules instead of coils.

trial.title: Measure the speed of sound with an echo
trial.lead: Sound is a wave, and a wave that bounces back is an **echo**. Here the echo keeps the time for you: you clap, the sound runs to a wall and back, and you clap again just as the echo arrives. Then the time between claps is the **round trip** of the sound.
trial.safety: **Safety:** do this in a school yard, park or sports field, **well away from roads and car parks**. Look where you walk and stay clear of the wall. Clapping is all the noise you need: no horns, whistles or bangs.
trial.need: **You need:** a big flat wall (a school wall or sports hall side) with about {eD} m of open ground in front of it, a tape measure or trundle wheel (or measure one stride and count strides), a stopwatch (a phone is fine) and a friend to time.
trial.steps:
**Do this:**
1. Stand a measured distance **d** from the wall (aim for about {eD} m). Clap once and listen for the echo.
2. Clap again exactly when you hear the echo, then again on the next echo, and so on: **each clap lands on the echo of the one before**. You are aiming at a steady rhythm of about {eF} claps per second.
3. Your friend starts the stopwatch on one clap and stops it {eN} claps later (count {eN} gaps between claps).
4. Repeat three times and average the times. Then try clapping softer, and louder.
trial.measure: **Measure:** d (m) and the total time t (s) for N = {eN} claps. Between two claps the sound travels to the wall and back, a distance 2d, in a time t/N. So **v = 2d / (t/N) = 2d·N / t**.
trial.compare: **Compare with the chapter:** in air at 20 °C, v = {soundV} m/s, so each clap takes 2d/v = {eInt} s and {eN} claps take about **{eT} s**. A stopwatch time between {eTlo} s and {eThi} s gives a speed between {eVlo} and {eVhi} m/s: good for a stopwatch. Clapping softer or louder should not change the time: **the medium sets v, not the amplitude**.
trial.wrong: **What goes wrong:** your reaction time delays both the start and the stop of the stopwatch, so the errors mostly cancel, and timing more claps makes the leftover error a smaller fraction. If your rhythm drifts you start clapping on the wrong echo, so listen for the echo of the clap just before. Closer than about {eD} m the claps must come too fast to keep up. Other walls give extra echoes, and on a cold day sound is a little slower.
